CHN.note: China is now counted on its own national statistics (260 TWh, 2024) rather than the IEA's 100 TWh. The two are not a disagreement about arithmetic — they are different universes. 260 TWh against the IEA's 31.9 GW of counted capacity implies a load factor of 0.93, which is physically impossible: nothing draws 93% of nameplate every hour of the year. So the Chinese figure must cover facilities the IEA's capacity count excludes, most likely telecom and 5G network rooms. China's own narrower series bears that out: the National Energy Administration reported 49.4 TWh for the internet data services industry in the first half of 2026, and the China Electricity Council said on Sep 16, 2026 that the half year was already close to the full-year 2024 level for that classification — about a fifth of the 260 TWh used here for the same year. Using it makes China's own number right and makes cross-country comparison looser. A third official reading now sits between the two. The National Energy Administration said on May 29, 2026 that China's computing centers used 170 TWh in 2025, 1.6% of national electricity - neither the narrow internet data services series nor the 260 TWh total. Against the same 31.9 GW it implies 170/(31.9 x 8.76) = 0.61 rather than 0.93, which is physically plausible, but it is 2025 energy against a capacity basis that is 2024 throughout, and it comes from a statement at a conference rather than a statistical release with a stated scope. It is recorded in policy.json and not used.
